title: What happened when I connected Claude to a live-stream of financial data
author: SnowSilent7695
selftext:
I've been wanting to track the market closely on a day-to-day basis and have always been curious about what would happen If had Claude listen to the market all day long. My primary goal was not have it trade or actively pick stocks, but to see how well it could short-list ideas from possibly hundreds of events that cross the tape. I had Claude stream live data to Claude Dashboards this morning, with it screening 81 events and highlighting ten. From this list, EAT and KIDS jumped out, and I ended up taking a position in both (great businesses and away from the AI noise, which I particularly like these days). 

I find that this has been great way so far to explore stocks that normally might not cross my radar.

I've made this experiment/project public. Anyone is welcome to view and clone the project to make it their own: [https://github.com/cbecks1212/flexreport-mcp](https://github.com/cbecks1212/flexreport-mcp)

You can also connect it straight to Claude: Customize > Connectors > Add custom connector > [https://mcp.flexreportfinapi.com/mcp](https://mcp.flexreportfinapi.com/mcp) \> This lets Claude stream real-time events.

I hope you have the same aha moment I had earlier this morning.

comments.body: the earnings-timestamp thread earlier this month was yours, I think. the number I'd keep isn't which two you bought, it's what the other 71 did: a week on, score the 10 against the 71 it passed over. if the highlighted set isn't ahead, the shortlist is a prettier way of reading the tape. the step after the shortlist is what Quantradin covers, I built it so the agent runs the idea as a written rule, fake money, and the screening and the buying get graded apart. quantradin.com. what did the 10 share that the 71 lacked, a catalyst type or just the size of the move?

replies.author: spoidercide
replies.body:
Yes exactly and did it beat buy and hold or random entry

Everyone wants to think their idea and when they're shown it's on a needle or overfit they don't go down the rabbit hole of why and give up

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: random entry is the harsher of the two and the one I'd run first: buy and hold on the same bars tells you about the market, random entries with the same holding period tell you whether the picking did anything. and yes, the rabbit hole is the product, the pretty shortlist is the exit.

comments.author: fleatedplutmting
comments.body:
I’d be just as interested in the 71 events it filtered out. Reviewing those alongside the shortlist would tell you whether it’s consistently finding useful information or occasionally missing something you’d have wanted to see.

The timestamps would matter too. When did the news hit, when did Claude flag it, and how much had the price already moved? That  helps distinguish early discovery from a convincing explanation of something already happening.

Since your goal is expanding your radar, I’d judge it partly on whether it surfaces businesses worth researching, regardless of their next days return.

Did you define what deserved a place on the shortlist or let Claude establish its own criteria ?

comments.author: RussFaigen
comments.body:
Cool experiment, and I like that you framed it as a shortlisting tool rather than "Claude picks stocks." Screening 81 events down to 10 is a job LLMs are actually decent at.



On the question someone asked about real-time data without a broker or paid feed: worth separating two things. An events stream (news, filings, earnings headlines) is different from live quotes. Your connector looks like it's streaming events, which can be close to real time. Actual live prices usually come from one of three places:

\- A paid market data vendor

\- Your broker's API, since most brokers with an API give account holders quote data

\- Free sources, which are often delayed, so check the timestamp before trusting them



For a shortlisting workflow, a little delay probably doesn't matter. If you ever let it act on price, it matters a lot.



The other commenter's idea is the one I'd actually do next. Log all 81 events with Claude's verdict and reasoning, then check how the 10 flagged vs the 71 skipped did over a week or a month. If the flagged ones don't beat the skipped ones, the model is telling good stories, not filtering. Do that over a few weeks and you'll have a real answer instead of two picks that happened to catch your eye.



Thanks for open-sourcing it, more people should share the setup instead of just the results.
